newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss 1996 machinery sector orders fell 8.6 pct.
newsitem.headline: Swiss 1996 machinery sector orders fell 8.6 pct.

text.p: Orders for Swiss machinery fell 8.6 percent in 1996 and foreign orders dropped for the first time since 1991, two industry groups said, adding western European economies held the key to the sector's prospects.

Data compiled by the Association of Swiss Engineering Employers and the Swiss Association of Machinery Manufacturers showed turnover fell 3.1 percent last year, but exports rose 2.7 percent thanks to solid order inflow in 1995.
"One can expect business activity to revive only when economies in western Europe recover," they said in a joint statement detailing their survey of 180 companies.
It said the Swiss franc's welcome decline had not yet spurred orders, which was understandable given enormous price pressure and weak demand.
"Many exporters must thus, swallow price cuts without being able to buy more volume growth," it said.

"The modestly positive economic forecasts for western European markets and the weaker Swiss franc should create better conditions for business activity from the second half of the year (1997)," it said.
"Structural adjustments that have been adopted steadily may also have a positive impact."

Total orders fell in all four quarters of 1996, it said, with foreign orders off 14.6 percent in the fourth quarter alone. Domestic orders were down 6.6 percent last year due to the poor investment environment in Switzerland, it added.
Asian markets provided the most impetus for exports in 1996, with sales to Singapore up 55 percent, to Indonesia 24 percent, to South Korea 17 percent and to Japan 15 percent.

Exports to the United States, Switzerland's second-largest market, rose four percent, while sales to main market Germany fell 2.5 percent. Good demand from Britain helped keep exports to the European Union roughly steady, at up 0.4 percent.
Although overall 1996 turnover fell 3.1 percent, sales in the fourth quarter rose 1.8 percent.
Work on hand dropped to a record low 4.0 months, due primarily to reduced processing times and market pressure.
